chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! I have a neighbour who is frequent in salat, frequent in charity, and frequent in hajj — there is nothing wrong with him.' So he said, 'O Is'haq, how is his intellect?' I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you — he has no intellect.' So he said, '(His deeds) will not be elevated for him because of that.'

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be sacrificed for you — a phrase of reverence and devotion used by companions when addressing the Imams
key_terms.عَقْل: intellect/reason ('aql) — in Shia theology, the divinely-granted faculty of discernment that determines the moral and spiritual value of human actions; one of the two fundamental principles of this chapter (the other being jahl/ignorance)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no problem/fault with him — an idiomatic expression meaning the person appears upright and commendable
key_terms.لَا يَرْتَفِعُ: will not be elevated — referring to the spiritual rank or station that cannot be raised without the foundation of intellect

ai.seo_question: Does performing prayer, charity, and hajj without intellect benefit a person according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith, Is'haq ibn Ammar describes a neighbor to Imam al-Sadiq (AS) as being devout in prayer, charity, and pilgrimage, yet the Imam immediately inquires about the man's intellect. When Is'haq reveals the man lacks intellect, the Imam declares that these acts of worship cannot elevate the man's status. This teaching belongs to the famous 'Kitab al-Aql wa-l-Jahl' (Book of Intellect and Ignorance), the opening chapter of al-Kafi, which emphasizes that the 'aql (intellect) is the foundational criterion by which all human acts are measured — without it, even seemingly virtuous deeds have no spiritual weight.
